nameStory: Tripora gets its name from the Greek 'tri' meaning three and 'poros' meaning passage or pore, likely referring to some three-part structure in its tiny flowers. The species name 'divaricata' means 'spreading widely apart,' describing how its branches stretch out at wide angles from the main stem.
description: Tripora is an extremely rare Asian member of the mint family that has somehow found its way to New England, with only a handful of sightings recorded. Like other mint family plants, it has square stems and opposite leaves, but it's quite different from our familiar native mints. This small herbaceous plant produces delicate flowers and has the characteristic aromatic qualities you'd expect from a mint relative, though much more subtle than kitchen herbs.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel distinctly four-sided when you roll them between your fingers - a telltale mint family trait that's very pronounced in this species

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves (pairs facing each other along the stem) that release a faint, pleasant herbal scent when gently crushed between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, delicate flowers that are much less showy than typical garden mints, appearing in loose clusters along the stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Branches spread at wide angles from the main stem, creating an open, airy appearance quite different from the upright growth of most mints

habitat: Given its extreme rarity in New England, specific habitat preferences here are unclear, but it likely prefers disturbed areas, garden edges, or waste places where other non-native plants establish. In its native Asian range, it grows in mountainous regions and forest margins.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with the characteristic square stems and opposite leaf arrangement becoming evident as the plant establishes.
seasonality.summer: Flowering period when the small, inconspicuous blooms appear and the plant reaches its full size for identification.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the plant begins to decline, though stems may persist showing the square structure.
seasonality.winter: Likely dies back completely, leaving no above-ground parts for identification.

funFact: This plant is so rare in New England that there are only 5 recorded observations - you're more likely to spot a rare bird than find this elusive mint family member growing wild!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small mint family plants, but the wide-spreading branch pattern and extremely subtle flowers help distinguish it from our common native mints like wild bergamot or catnip, which have much showier blooms and different growth habits.
contextualKnowledge: You might still see this plant listed under its old scientific name Caryopteris divaricata in older field guides or online resources, as the name change to Tripora happened relatively recently in 1999.
compareHints: Since Tripora is the only species in its genus, compare it to other mint family members. Unlike showy relatives like bee balm or the aromatic kitchen mints, Tripora has much more subtle flowers and fragrance. Its wide-spreading growth habit also sets it apart from the typically upright growth of most mint family plants.
